newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court dismisses line-item veto challenge.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court dismisses line-item veto challenge.

text.p: The Supreme Court on Thursday dismissed a legal challenge by six members of Congress to a law that greatly expands the president's power to veto individual spending and tax items.
The high court ruled by a 7-2 vote that the legislators who sued in challenging the historic line-item veto law lacked the legal standing or right to bring the case in the first place.
President Bill Clinton has yet to use his expanded veto power under the law, which took effect in January. A U.S. District Court judge in April struck down the law as unconstitutional.

"We hold that (the lawmakers) lack standing to bring this suit and therefore direct that the judgment of the district court be vacated and the complaint dismissed," Chief Justice William Rehnquist declared for the court majority.
One dissenter, Justice John Paul Stevens, said he would declare the law unconstitutional.
The other dissenter, Justice Stephen Breyer, said he thought the case could be decided, and expressed no view on the merits of the law, "reserving them for future argument."
Clinton hailed the decision, saying he plannned to use the line-item veto power "whenever appropriate" and that he looked forward "to using it wisely."

He said the decision cleared the way for him to "use this valuable tool for eliminating waste in the federal budget and for enlivening the public debate over how to make the best use of public funds."
Although the court sidestepped a decision on the law's constitutionality, it ultimately could rule on that question in a case once Clinton actually vetoes an item.
Opponents who brought the case, including Rep. David Skaggs, a Colorado Democrat, predicted that they will ultimately prevail.

"This is a lawsuit that someone will soon win," Skaggs said. "There are many ways to cut wasteful spending but there is only one Constitution. It prescribes the rules for making laws and the line-item veto statute violates those rules."

The law allows the president to strip items from spending measures without vetoing the entire bill. Presidents of both parties had long coveted the power because it vastly expands their room for maneuver in budget negotiations and has been viewed as a powerful tool to reduce the U.S. budget deficit.
The law was adopted last year by the Republican Congress as part of the party's "Contract with America" and was strongly supported by Clinton.

Besides Skaggs, the law was challenged in court by Sens. Robert Byrd of West Virginia, Carl Levin of Michigan, Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York and Mark Hatfield of Oregon and Rep. Henry Waxman of California.
All are Democrats except Hatfield, a Republican who retired from Congress after the suit was filed in January.
The lawmakers claimed in their lawsuit that the line-item veto violated the process set out by the Constitution for Congress and the presidency on how legislation becomes law.
The high court agreed with the Justice Department argument that the legislators lacked standing to sue because they had not suffered any concrete, personal injury from the yet-to-be-used law.

Rehnquist said the Supreme Court insists on strict compliance with its standing requirements, especially in a dispute involving the constitutionality of a law affecting the powers of the various branches of government.

He said the lawmakers could not claim institutional injury, noting they had not been authorized by the House or Senate to represent their respective body in the lawsuit. "Indeed, both (chambers) actively oppose their suit," he said.
Rehnquist said members of Congress have a possible remedy for their complaints about the law -- they could repeal it.
